title: Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts
one_liner: A pool of remote nurses that acts as the recorded, independent second person on video for narcotic waste, blood checks and high-alert drug double-checks when a rural hospital has three nurses on at 3am.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals (25 beds or fewer, roughly 1,300 in the US), plus the malpractice and captive insurers that cover them. Hospitals pay a monthly subscription.
problem: Policy requires a second licensed person to witness controlled-substance waste and to independently double-check insulin, heparin, blood and pediatric doses. At night at a rural hospital that second person is a nurse who is mid-code or mid-admission. Every nurse knows the witness signature is often given without actually watching. That is the most common way nurses divert drugs, and it is also how honest nurses end up with paper trails that would not survive an audit. The hospital cannot prove the witness happened. The other option is waking a colleague from another unit, which delays care.
solution: Start with a $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet. A remote RN appears on video within 60 seconds, watches the waste happen, and attests in a portal. The system keeps a time-stamped video clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet's waste records, exported as a PDF for the diversion committee. Then add two-RN blood transfusion verification, independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, and a 'second set of eyes' call for pediatric dosing. Do no EHR integration at first. Matching by timestamp is enough to sell.
why_now: The Bluesight 2026 State of Hospital Pharmacy report says about 63% of health-system leaders reported at least one diversion incident in the past year, and waste is a top diversion method because witnessing is loosely policed. Virtual nursing has become normal since 2024, and the Nurse Licensure Compact now covers most states, so one remote nurse can cover many hospitals. State Rural Health Transformation Program money is flowing, with every state having posted at least one funding opportunity by August 2026, and workforce and quality dollars can pay for this. Whether remote-video witnessing is acceptable is mostly a hospital-policy and pharmacy and therapeutics committee decision, but each state's board of pharmacy and nursing board should be checked before launch.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month, plus a per-event fee for transfusion and double-check calls above a set volume. A typical rural ED has 10-25 waste events a night at 2-3 minutes each, so one remote RN can cover roughly 8-12 hospitals per night. Estimated gross margin is 40-50%. A secondary revenue line is a discount arrangement with medical liability insurers, who benefit from the audit trail.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone selling diversion software (analytics, cabinet data mining, waste-testing) tries to detect diversion after the fact. Insiders know the root problem is that no real second person exists at night in a small hospital. You do not need better detection. You need to supply the missing colleague, cheaply and on camera. The service also protects honest nurses, who will therefore support it and not resist it.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses who want remote night hours at $35-40/hr. Use an off-the-shelf tablet with a recording app and a simple web portal that produces the PDF log. Offer free 30-day pilots to two critical access hospitals through the founder nurse's own pharmacy director and CNO. Get the pilot approved as a policy amendment at the pharmacy and therapeutics committee. Convert to a $1,500 monthly contract after 30 days if the audit log is shown to the diversion committee and the hospital's insurer.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing.

title: Phantom Pipeline Audits for Utility Rate-Case Intervenors
one_liner: Sell to the ratepayers who pay for phantom load, meaning industrial customer groups and state consumer advocates in IRP, CPCN and large-load-tariff dockets, a testimony-ready audit of how much of a utility's confidential data-center pipeline is physically real.
customer: Buyer: counsel and expert budgets of (a) industrial customer intervenor groups (steel, paper, chemicals) that fear being left with stranded data-center infrastructure costs, and (b) state consumer advocate offices, in dockets where the utility's generation or transmission request rests on a data-center pipeline. Later: county and city governments facing abatement votes ($15-30K packs), and utility credit and equity analysts who subscribe to a Phantom Ratio Index. The sales path is through the law firms and staff attorneys who run these dockets.
problem: Utilities are asking commissions to approve gigawatts of gas plants and transmission justified by 'signed' large-load pipelines. The pipeline exhibits are confidential or anonymized ('Customer A, 400 MW'). Intervenor experts can only critique them top-down with econometrics, because nobody checks entries one by one against the physical trail. The evidence that pipelines are inflated is broad: an EPRI survey found none of 10 utilities with requests of 50%+ of peak expected actual 5-year load above 35% of peak, and Exelon's estimates fell about 40% after stricter collateral. But the intervenor cannot show which megawatts are fake, and a project shopped to two utilities is counted twice.
solution: A 'realization audit' delivered through counsel. Under the docket's protective order, the desk takes the utility's pipeline exhibit (MW, county or substation, in-service date, status). It scores each entry against the public trail: air permits and generator counts, deed or option and rezoning agenda items, water and stormwater filings, principal and LLC cross-matching across states, and whether the claimed in-service date is feasible given published equipment lead times. The output is a probability-weighted realized MW by year with confidence bands, a list of duplicate-counted megawatts across utilities, and a testimony-ready exhibit sponsored by a credentialed expert witness (a retired utility planner or former commission staffer on retainer). Where entries are fully anonymized, the audit triangulates from county-level permit and land-use activity and asks the commission to compel the identities under protective order. The same work product seeds a quarterly Phantom Ratio Index by utility and state.
why_now: Electricity affordability is a live political issue in the November 2026 midterms, and data-center load forecasts are the key contested input in a wave of 2026 large-load tariff, IRP and generation-certificate dockets. Regulators are already moving on transparency (Texas ownership audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW), so intervenors now have standing to ask for pipeline detail. Cleanview-style permit trackers plus OCR'd county records have made the public-trail checks cheap enough to run per docket at a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $40-120K fixed fee per docket engagement, covering the audit, exhibit and expert sponsorship, paid from intervenor budgets and industrial group dues. $15-30K county and municipal packs. A $25-60K/yr Phantom Ratio Index seat for credit analysts, muni and equity desks and hedge funds. Year-1 target: 6-10 dockets ($600K-$900K) plus early index subscribers, with about 60% gross margin because the expert and analyst time is billable.
non_obvious_insight: The parties who lose most from phantom load are not the utility's five planners but the other ratepayers, and they already have lawyers, a procedural calendar and an expert budget. The docket schedule sets the deadline, so no procurement cycle is needed. The natural competitors, utility-aligned engineering consultancies, are conflicted when the audit target is their client's pipeline, which makes an adversarial audit counter-positioned rather than just different. And duplicate-counting is only visible from outside: each utility sees only its own queue, but an auditor working in four states sees the same project in three pipelines. The adversarial work therefore seeds the national duplicate registry from a side no utility-aligned vendor can reach.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every live docket in 6-8 states where a large-load pipeline is in dispute, using public commission dockets, and note testimony deadlines in the next 60-120 days plus who the intervenors and their counsel are. Days 10-20: build a free 2-page 'public trail check' of one utility's publicly disclosed data-center announcements, using licensed permit data plus deeds and permits, and send it to 15 intervenor counsel and consumer advocate staff. Recruit a credentialed expert witness (retired planner or ex-commission staff). Days 20-30: close 1-2 paid engagements at about $40K, one with an industrial group and one with a consumer advocate. Kill test: if counsel will not pay $40K for a per-entry audit because their econometric expert already covers it, the intervenor thesis is dead and the index is the fallback.

title: Outside-In Product Security Ratings for Insurers and Buyers
one_liner: Invert the desk: instead of helping one maker meet the 24-hour clock, independently measure from the outside whether thousands of connected-product makers can, and how exposed their shipped firmware is, and sell the scores and accumulation data to insurers, fleet buyers and lenders.
customer: First buyers: cyber and product-liability insurers and MGAs writing hardware and IoT makers, who need product-level exposure and accumulation data. Second: B2B fleet and infrastructure buyers (EV-charging operators, micromobility fleets, smart-building integrators, telcos buying CPE) that run supplier due diligence. Third: lenders and PE firms doing diligence on hardware brands. Manufacturers do not buy scores. They pay only for evidence review and remediation (a funnel to the desk).
problem: Every maker will soon say 'we comply' with the CRA, but the declarations are self-assessed and unverified until a market surveillance authority acts, which is slow and under-resourced. Insurers have no product-level model of accumulation, even though one exploited component hits every device on that stack. That is a catastrophe-modelling problem with no model. Procurement teams rely on questionnaires. The 24-hour clock is uniquely measurable: it is a dated, binary behaviour, unlike vague 'security posture', but nobody measures it from outside.
solution: A rating built outside-in from three layers. (a) Clock-readiness signals: security.txt, a published CVD policy, a working vulnerability contact, advisory history, stated support period, update cadence, and time-to-acknowledge on a clearly labelled contact-verification probe. (b) Firmware exposure: public firmware and OTA images, plus purchased units for top SKUs, unpacked and matched against exploited-vulnerability feeds to give a component list, exposure count and stack cluster. (c) Portfolio accumulation: for an insurer's book of insureds or a fleet buyer's supplier list, how many share a stack with a newly exploited component (the correlation number). Makers get a right of reply and can submit evidence, but cannot pay to change a score. Method: month 0-3 process-signal ratings for about 500 brands across e-mobility, smart home, routers, chargers, cameras and wearables; month 3-6 firmware exposure on the top 200 SKUs and the first accumulation reports. A separate analyst team runs the desk as the remediation upsell, behind a conflict-of-interest firewall.
why_now: The reporting duty went live on 11 Sep 2026, so 'time to report' just became a legal, checkable behaviour. Insurers are pricing CRA-driven product liability for the first time. Outside-in ratings are a proven category for company networks, and firmware unpacking is now cheap through open-source tooling and LLM-assisted triage. No dominant product-level rating exists.
revenue_model: Data licences of EUR 25-80k/yr per insurer or MGA; EUR 6-15k/yr per fleet operator or integrator per category; EUR 3-8k per diligence report for lenders and PE; EUR 2-5k per maker for evidence review; desk upsell as a funnel. Long term the rating is written into insurance pricing and procurement clauses ('supplier must hold a score of B or better'), giving standard-setter economics with a data moat.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers care about accumulation more than any single score, and the desk's pooled stack graph is exactly an accumulation model, so the same data serves the desk and the rating. Real filings and drills, with consent and anonymised, give a calibration set showing which outside-in signals predict actual time-to-report, and that validation is what makes a rating credible. Every desk client both funds and calibrates the rating. Flaw of the inversion: legal risk (defamation, unauthorised access), which is why probes are labelled, analysis uses lawfully obtained units and public images, scores are aggregated and methodology is public.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: build a crawler over 500 brands in 6 categories to score security.txt, CVD page, contact deliverability, advisory history and support-period statements. Week 2: send a benign, clearly labelled contact-verification probe and record response times. Week 3: publish a free report, 'State of vulnerability-reporting readiness among 500 connected-product brands' (for example, what share have no working vulnerability contact weeks after the duty began), to earn press and insurer attention. Weeks 3-4: hold 20 discovery calls with cyber/product-liability underwriters, MGAs and fleet operators, and offer paid pilots of EUR 8-15k to score their insureds or suppliers. Aim for one signed pilot by day 45 and confirm that no insurer-grade product rating already exists before scaling.
lineage: mutation of I0374 ('Outsourced 24-Hour Vulnerability Reporting Desk (CRA)'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service), Finite State (managed CRA service), Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service), Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source). White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure. | How this version avoids them: The parent's competitors (Finite State, Cybellum, ONEKEY, Cybeats, CVD Portal, CRA Evidence, CRACI) all work inside-out for the manufacturer's own firmware or workflow and are paid by the maker. This business is outside-in and paid by the party that bears the risk, so none of them competes for that buyer, and several become data suppliers. From general knowledge, not verified in this session: company-level ratings such as BitSight and SecurityScorecard score networks, not shipped products; certification schemes (ioXt, ETSI EN 303 645-based tests, UL programmes) are pass/fail, point-in-time and manufacturer-paid; consumer-testing NGOs publish periodic tests. Large MSSPs and certification bodies are conflicted because manufacturers pay them. The moat is the calibrated stack graph, the methodology and eventual adoption in insurance and procurement contracts.

title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.
customer: Laid-off ops, finance and product managers with severance or savings of about $100-300K, who pay cohort tuition and a success fee. Second customer: retiring owners of scrap and recycling businesses who want a successor buyer. SBA lenders are a channel.
problem: Mid-career job searches now run 7-13 months with near-zero interview rates (HN threads), and the hiring freeze is hitting degree-holders. Meanwhile thousands of owner-run recycling businesses have no successor. Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.
solution: Build a target database from state solid-waste and hazardous-waste permit records, scrap-dealer licenses and owner age. Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing a large pool of capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: In recycling the scarce input is not technology or capital but a competent successor operator, and the labor market is now manufacturing them. Permits are the moat, so the right move is to buy permitted cash flow instead of financing new plants.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states. Run a free webinar for laid-off managers through layoff-tracker and career communities and enroll a first cohort of about 10. Get two retiring owners to sign exclusive sell-side LOIs. Sign an environmental-consulting partner for a flat-fee diligence pack, and one SBA lender as the financing partner.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Search Fund Accelerator (SFA), Kingsway Search Xcelerator (KSX), Codie Sanchez / Contrarian Thinking ('boring business' acquisition education), University ETA programs and search fund ecosystem (Stanford GSB, Kellogg, WashU Olin, Yale, Cleveland ETA program). White space: I found no scrap, recycling or transfer-station-specific acquisition accelerator. Every searcher or ETA program I could verify is sector-agnostic, and none packages this asset class for a first-time buyer. That is limited evidence. The session's 200-call WebSearch budget was already spent. I fell back on Google News RSS, the Hacker News API, the Federal Register API and direct fetches, and could not reach Crunchbase, Product Hunt, Reddit, Searchfunder or BizBuySell.

What looks unserved:
1. A vertical diligence and financing pack for sub-$5M scrap and recycling yards. It would cover Phase I/II and fire-history checks, insurance, permit transferability and offtake contracts. Horizontal ETA programs leave that to each buyer. Fire and insurance risk is live: EMR's Camden yard was shut after 15 fires in six years (NJ PEN, 29 May 2026), Resource Recycling wrote 'Battery fire risk isn't going away. Insurance is responding' (24 Feb 2026), and a 9,000-car Idaho salvage yard burned (Yahoo, 19 Jun 2026).
2. A succession desk for owner-run yards. Nothing I found targets ReMA-type family operators with a packaged successor, and the big consolidators only want larger yards.
3. A permit-and-owner-age target list. Nothing I found offers one for scrap dealers.

The premise needs two corrections:
- The BIS rule is real. It is a temporary final rule, published 6 Aug 2026 and effective 27 Aug 2026. However, it covers only black mass and tungsten waste and scrap, not ordinary ferrous or nonferrous yards (Federal Register 2026-16078). The 'domestic scrap re-rating' story is much narrower than the pitch implies.
- The idea leans on 'laid-off managers with $100-300K'. That is a crowded buyer-education market, with Codie Sanchez, Kingsway and the universities all courting the same buyers.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.

title: Record-on-Request Desk for Superior Courts
one_liner: A managed compliance service that lets a superior court answer any indigent litigant's request for a verbatim record with one certified record per request, priced per record delivered and using the cheapest lawful method, whether steno or electronic recording.
customer: Court executive officers and presiding family/probate judges of small and mid-size California superior courts, especially those outside the AB 3013 pilot or above its 10-20% cap. Self-represented litigants and DV legal aid are the users, but the court is the payer.
problem: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) gives indigent litigants a mandatory right to an official verbatim record on request, through court-paid pro tem reporters or electronic recording. Courts have no reporters and hiring freezes, and they cannot staff for requests that could arrive any day. Their real gap is a defensible request-to-record workflow: intake, indigency check, method selection, delivery of a certified appeal-ready record, and reporting. The 3 million hearings without a record are already a Judicial Council-visible metric. Half-day pro tem minimums make each request cost $450-500 or more.
solution: A per-request desk, priced by outcome. The litigant or facilitator files a request when they set the hearing, so the desk usually gets 2-7 days of notice, which turns random demand into schedulable demand. The desk picks the method: (a) the court's own recording plus a certified transcript on demand (subcontracted to an eScribers-style vendor), or (b) a physically present steno reporter from a pooled roster that covers several requests in the same courthouse (the offspring-1 network) when a steno record is required or the department has no recording. The court pays only for records delivered and certified. A dashboard shows requests, turnaround and no-record rate by department, ready for Judicial Council reporting. The desk is offered at no retainer with a quarterly spend cap, sized to the court's own budget.
why_now: The Supreme Court decision is Aug 2026 and the court decision names the compliance routes, so every court now needs a plan, and no incumbent has packaged one. Reporter budgets and vacancy savings exist because courts cannot fill positions, and CA has already sent dedicated funding to court reporters (verify the current allocation and whether vacancy savings can be redirected). Verbit's Judicial Council master agreement for captioning from July 1, 2026 shows courts do buy court-tech through master agreements, which gives a path from single-court pilots to statewide.
revenue_model: The court pays a flat $150-250 per hearing record delivered (up to 30 minutes), certified transcripts at a per-page rate, and no retainer. Pricing sits below a $450-500 half-day pro tem and far below an idle full-time reporter. Steno requests use pooled reporters, and audio requests use subcontracted transcription, so gross margin is about 30-40%. Year 2: annual subscription for the dashboard and intake software, and a statewide master-agreement bid. Legal aid and foundations can fund 'request navigators' who file requests for litigants, which lifts volume.
non_obvious_insight: The court does not need reporters. It needs a defensible answer to a request, so the method is irrelevant, and the biggest threat (electronic recording) becomes a supply input to a desk that will choose it. Requests that arrive at intake instead of at the courtroom door are what make pooled steno economical, because notice converts unpredictable demand into a schedule. Outcome pricing ('pay only when a certified record is delivered') is the contingency that lets a risk-averse court say yes without a retainer.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney, plus reading the ruling's list of lawful compliance routes. Weeks 1-3: ask FVAP and 2-3 DV legal-aid groups to introduce court executives of two counties with the highest no-record rates. Build the intake form and an eScribers-style subcontract, and sign 3 physical pro tem reporters in one county. Weeks 3-4: offer one family department a no-cost, at-cost 60-day compliance pilot (about 20-40 requests) with a weekly report. Aim for an under-threshold purchase order or sole-source urgent-compliance pilot within 90-120 days. The 30-day success test is a signed pilot letter from one court and a design-partner agreement with FVAP.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind. | How this version avoids them: Steno, DirectDep and StenoScout sell to attorneys, mostly depositions, and have no intake, indigency, certification or reporting workflow for courts. The incumbent agencies sell courts half-day pro tem bookings, which is the price the desk undercuts. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings but do not handle request intake, method choice or physical steno backup, so they are supply partners, not rivals. The AB 3013 pilot is court-employed, capped and in 13 counties; we serve every court above the cap or outside the pilot. The main threat is a court building intake in-house or a Judicial Council master agreement commoditizing the service, so the plan is to be on the master agreement's vendor list early and to own the request-intake data.

title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead.

title: AP-Inbox Implant Reconciler for Spine ASCs
one_liner: Forward your implant vendor invoices to one email address. We match each to the surgery, the payer's carve-out clause and the 835, and reopen the claim the day the invoice lands, so implant cost stops going unpaid.
customer: Independent, surgeon-owned spine and pain-management (spinal cord stimulator) ASCs doing about 100-600 implant cases a year. They have a one-to-three-person in-house billing office, or an outsourced biller paid a percentage of collections, and no supply-chain analyst. The buyer is the administrator plus the surgeon-owner who signs off on distributions. Launch in one state through its ASC association so outreach is dense.
problem: The leak is not ignorance of carve-outs (Becker's has covered them since 2014). It is a hand-off race. The claim leaves billing days after surgery. The consignment vendor invoice lands in accounts payable weeks later, if it is ever tied to the case. Sticker-sheet lot numbers, invoice lines and payer attachment rules share no common ID. So the claim goes out at charges, posts as 'paid', and no system emits the event 'invoice arrived for a case already billed'. Corrected-claim and appeal windows then expire silently. Testable hypothesis for the first audits: a meaningful share of implant cases have a claim date earlier than the invoice date. Each miss is worth roughly $5k-30k, and Medicare ASC cases are excluded because they are not carved out.
solution: (1) Zero-integration intake. Vendor invoices are auto-forwarded from the AP inbox, QuickBooks or Bill.com. An LLM extracts line items (manufacturer, catalog, lot, UDI-DI, unit price). The case schedule or implant log comes as a CSV or photos of sticker sheets, and the ERAs are pulled from the clearinghouse. No EHR or practice-management integration. (2) Rule engine with a payer-clause library. Contract PDFs are LLM-extracted and human-verified once, then reused across every ASC with the same payer. For workers' comp and no-fault, the engine uses public state fee schedules, several of which pay implants at invoice cost plus a capped markup (verify per state). This removes the 'read every contract' scaling limit. (3) The trigger. When an invoice matches a case already billed at $0 or bundled, it auto-builds the payer-specific attachment packet and corrected claim or appeal, ranked by days left to timely filing. Coders file for the first year, then automation. (4) A weekly one-page 'implant cash gap' for the administrator: unmatched invoices, invoice lag by vendor, payers paying $0.
why_now: ASC volume is shifting toward device-heavy musculoskeletal cases. CMS's CY2026 ASC final rule (CMS-1834-FC) is reported to add more of them; verify the exact list. Becker's ran 'ASCs' implant cost problem' in March 2026 and 'payer terms ASCs can't miss' in July 2026. Payer AI payment-integrity tools now auto-zero claims that lack attachments. LLM invoice extraction, which used to need OCR templates per vendor, is now cents per invoice.
revenue_model: Lookback: 25% of cash actually collected on recovered carve-outs, over a 12-18 month lookback bounded by timely filing, with no fee if nothing is recovered. Then convert to $1.5-2.5k/month per ASC (or about $12 per implant case) for the invoice trigger and weekly digest. Hypothesis to prove in the audits: a 300-implant-case ASC with a 10% leak at about $8k a case is $240k a year, so about $60k of first-year contingency and $18-30k a year of recurring revenue. Fifty ASCs would be roughly $1M+ of ARR plus about $3M of one-time contingency.
non_obvious_insight: The missing thing is an event, not data. Every RCM tool is triggered from the billing side, and nothing in the stack fires when an invoice arrives in AP after the claim is gone. Accounts payable is also the cheapest integration surface in healthcare, since forwarding email needs no IT project, so time-to-first-dollar is days. The wedge also counter-positions against billers. A percentage-of-collections biller cannot sell 'your billing is incomplete' without indicting itself, and the AP-side product never asks to replace them.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM or call 40 spine/SCS ASC administrators and surgeon-owners in one state via its ASC association and LinkedIn, offering a free 12-month lookback at 25% of cash collected only. Sign 3 design partners with a BAA. Week 2: pull 12 months of 835s, case and implant logs, and the AP invoice folder. Extract invoices with an LLM and spot-check to at least 95% line accuracy. Hand-read each site's top 3 commercial carve-out clauses. Week 3: match and measure three things. These are the share of implant cases where the claim predates the invoice, the implant lines paid $0 or bundled where the clause says carve-out, and the dollars still inside timely filing. Week 4: file the first 15-25 corrected claims and appeals, write a one-page anonymized leak report, and start outbound to 40 more ASCs. Gate: continue only if at least 2 of 3 sites show identifiable, collectible leakage of at least 3% of implant spend. Otherwise narrow to newly opened or converted ASCs, or kill.

None ingest vendor AP invoices or fire on invoice arrival, and they are retrospective variance tools, not per-case attachment and corrected-claim builders. This product is sold to the ASC owner and administrator as a supply-chain-to-cash control, which those enterprise sellers do not reach. SIS/Surgical Notes and HST Pathways sit in the practice-management and billing workflow that this product deliberately stays outside, so it works with any biller or PM system. Defensibility comes from the cross-ASC payer-clause library and invoice-lag dataset, which is a cornered resource, and from the switching cost of becoming the ASC's implant ledger. If Aspirion bolts on contract-level carve-outs, it still needs the AP-side intake and the ASC-owner sale.

title: Chute-Side Cow Counts for Ag Lenders
one_liner: Turn the vet's preg-check clipboard into a borrower-consented, third-party-verified herd inventory that banks can lend against.
customer: Community banks, Farm Credit associations and ag lenders with cattle loan books (they require it or pay per report, usually passed through to the borrower). Secondary payer is the cow-calf or heifer-development operator who wants bigger operating lines or bred-heifer financing on better terms.
problem: Cattle collateral has no VIN. Lenders verify with drive-by counts and borrower-supplied spreadsheets, and prosecutors in 2026 alleged a roughly $9.4M fraud that included a loan of $2.8M against 850 head. Farm loan delinquencies are rising while bred cows trade around $3,000+ per head, so a 500-cow borrower is $1.5M+ of collateral that nobody independent has counted.
solution: A 'Verified Herd Report' generated at the working day the vet is already doing. The vet or tech logs every head with an EID or visual tag scan (a $500 handheld reader plus a phone app), age class, pregnancy status and stage, and location. The vet e-signs and the borrower approves sharing with one tap. The lender gets a portal with timestamped, geotagged counts and year-over-year flags (head count down, pregnancy rate down, tags not matching last year). A second light pass happens at weaning. The vet earns a per-head fee for data they already write down and throw in the truck door pocket.
why_now: Federal EID ear tags became mandatory for many interstate cattle movements in Nov 2024, so per-head digital ID is now normal and cheap. Herd rebuilding at record cattle prices is being financed with debt, lenders entered 2026 carrying operating losses from 2023-2025 (rising delinquencies and restructures), and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case is making ag loan committees ask for verification. Fall preg-check season is running right now (Sept-Nov).
revenue_model: $2-3 per head per verification, split roughly 50/50 with the vet practice, charged to the borrower or the lender as a loan condition. Add a portfolio dashboard for lenders at $500-2,000 per month once an institution has 100+ verified borrowers. Later, sell the verified inventory and pregnancy data to lenders as an underwriting input (advance rates on verified bred heifers).
non_obvious_insight: The vet is the only independent professional who physically handles every animal in the herd once or twice a year. They count, tag-check and pregnancy-check every cow, and that data dies on a clipboard. Vets refuse to police clients, but they will happily attest to what they handled when the borrower initiates the request, so the conflict-of-interest problem disappears. Honest borrowers are the real buyers: verified bred females can justify higher advance rates, and that cheap capital funds the fee many times over.
first_30_days: Preg-check season is live, so sign up 3 rural practices that each do several thousand head of fall preg-checks. Pitch 3-4 community-bank ag lenders (target the one who has been burned by a herd count before; work through state bankers' association ag committees). Run a pilot on about 10 willing borrowers with a form-based app and a PDF report, charging $2/head. Gather a before and after on what the lender learned that the drive-by inspection missed, then use that to sell the annual program.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global / Where Food Comes From (Beef Passport), Merck Animal Health (Allflex tags/readers, Vence). White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature.

title: Dispatch-Eligibility Registry for Backup Generators
one_liner: Become the neutral system of record for whether each backup generator may legally run for the grid right now, starting as a Texas SB 6 compliance product and growing into the rail that ERCOT, PJM, utilities and aggregators check before dispatch.
customer: First buyer: environmental and compliance leads at 75 MW+ data centers in Texas, who face the SB 6 disclosure and deploy-on-direction duty and must not violate emissions limits. Then PJM colos that must prove permit compliance to state air agencies and counties. Then DR aggregators, utilities and RTOs that consume the dispatch-eligibility certificate through an API. Later expansion is to hospitals, water utilities and telecom, where the wider standby generator fleet is far larger (widely cited estimates run into the hundreds of GW, which I have not verified).
problem: Backup generation is the largest idle block of capacity, but it can only be called if three things are true at the moment of the call: the engine is permitted for that use, it has hours left in the rolling year, and the trigger is a legally recognized emergency. Today the answer sits in permit PDFs, OEM dashboards and spreadsheets. Regulators cannot see it, so they say no. Aggregators carry enforcement risk and cannot prove compliance. Communities suspect the worst about diesel, which sinks permits. Nobody can be sure that dispatching an engine on a given day will not breach a cap.
solution: A run-hour ledger and certificate service. Step one is software only: an ingest of permit conditions (LLM-structured, attorney-reviewed) plus monthly or continuous hour-meter data from BMS exports, OEM telemetry or a read-only J1939/Modbus tap, with non-resettable meter attestation as a fallback. It computes remaining permitted hours per engine, tags every run with its legal basis (test, maintenance, emergency, directed deployment), auto-generates regulator deviation and compliance reports, and publishes a public disclosure page. Step two is a machine-readable Dispatch Eligibility Certificate (open schema, mapped to OpenADR 3.0 and IEEE 2030.5 event payloads, which carry price and event signals but not legal eligibility). RTOs, utilities and aggregators query it before calling an engine. Step three, once regulators accept the format, is clearing and settlement of permit-cleared MW across the registry.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (2025) makes disclosure and directed deployment of backup generation a legal duty for 75 MW+ loads, with an explicit emissions carve-out, so demand for exactly this record is forced by regulation. PJM is filing a reliability backstop and connect-and-manage framework, and Pennsylvania is pushing bring-your-own-generation rules. Turbines are sold out to about 2029-30. LLM extraction of permit conditions cuts the cost of structuring each site from consultant weeks to hours plus attorney QA. None of this existed at scale in 2019.
revenue_model: Onboarding and permit structuring of $15-40k per facility. SaaS of $3-6k per engine per year, which is about $25-50k a year for a 20 MW fleet of 8-10 engines. Aggregators and utilities pay a verification fee of roughly 0.5-1% of dispatch revenue that runs through certificates, and lenders, insurers and RTOs license the data ($100-300k a year). Illustrative scale: 5,000 engines is about $20M ARR, and the roughly 22,000 data center engines implied by 55 GW at 2.5 MW each is about $90M. Wider standby fleets would multiply that several times.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce commodity is not megawatts or even permits. It is remaining permitted run-hours, a finite annual budget per engine, and nobody keeps that ledger neutrally. Whoever holds the ledger regulators trust becomes the rail everyone else must query, and the aggregators cannot build it because they profit from dispatch and cannot credibly police themselves. This inverts the parent: instead of pushing MW into the grid and hoping regulators follow, make regulators' comfort the product. Regulators have said no partly because they cannot see run hours. The registry supplies that visibility and could become the reason a permit is granted with conditions. It also creates network economies (every consumer of the certificate raises the value of being in it) and switching costs, since compliance history is an audit record.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ship a software-only SB 6 and Title V ledger MVP (permit parsing plus hour-meter ingest plus report generation) and publish the Dispatch Eligibility Certificate v0.1 schema openly. Days 5-30: contact compliance leads at 20 Texas 75 MW+ operators and offer five pilots at $15k with a fixed-format SB 6 backup-generation disclosure pack. Days 10-30: hold informal briefings with TCEQ and VA DEQ staff to test whether an electronic ledger is acceptable as a compliance record, and get consumption LOIs (free API in exchange for feedback) from at least one aggregator. The riskiest assumption is regulator acceptance, so test it in the first month. Retain an air attorney to review the legal-basis tagging.

The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

title: Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers

why_now: Multi-GW campuses, NERC's large-load task force and Texas and PJM interconnection rules in 2025-26 are turning load models from optional into a gating item.
revenue_model: $75-300k per project for the model and study, an annual model-maintenance subscription, and test or certification fees paid by UPS and power-shelf OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames data centers as demand. The grid now treats them as a dynamic device, like a giant inverter-based generator. title: Load-Proven Warranty Wrap for Data Halls
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of chasing OEMs for owners as warranties expire, run a standardized load-proof test before expiry, fix what the OEM owes for free, then sell a capacity-backed warranty wrap that covers the post-expiry tail, priced from a proprietary fleet failure database.
customer: First buyers: owners and lenders' technical advisors of energized data halls approaching OEM warranty expiry, asking for a standardized Load-Proven test and certificate (a covenant-friendly document for refinancing or ABS). Later buyers: the same owners buying multi-year coverage for gensets, UPS, chillers and liquid-cooling CDUs. The capacity provider (a specialty insurer or reinsurer) is a third party in the money flow.
problem: The parent's contingency model is hard to collect and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds. Behind that is a bigger issue: once OEM warranties lapse, owners of AI halls with dense power and liquid cooling carry an unpriced failure tail, and nobody has independent load-tested failure data on these systems. OEM service contracts cover a single vendor's gear and are priced generically. Lenders financing GPU-era assets see equipment residual risk with no standard way to test or rate it.
solution: Phase 1, within 6 months: sell a standardized Load-Proven protocol. It is a 3-5 day staged load test (gensets, UPS and battery, chillers and CDUs, breakers), thermography, oil, coolant and battery diagnostics, using a load-bank rental partner and NETA-type testing subcontractors. Each test outputs a certificate and, where a defect shows, an OEM claim package while the OEM is still liable. Every test feeds a proprietary failure and degradation database. Phase 2, months 6-18: place multi-year tail coverage for tested gear through a broker or MGA partner on a quota-share basis with an insurer or reinsurer. Only gear that passed the test is bound. Defects surfaced by the test are repaired at the OEM's cost first, so the wrap covers a cleaner tail. Phase 3: become the MGA, and push the test protocol into loan covenants and insurer schedules as the standard.
why_now: AI halls introduce liquid-cooling and high-density power gear with immature public failure data, so generic pricing is either too expensive or blind. Data center lending and ABS need equipment-condition standards. Phase slippage means a large group of halls will pass through OEM expiry without ever having been stressed. Cheap LLM extraction of test logs and maintenance records lets a small team standardize reports across sites.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $60-120K per hall for the Load-Proven test (much of it load-bank pass-through), plus any claim-based fee. Phase 2: broker commission, then MGA ceding and profit commission on premium. Assumed pricing to validate with capacity providers: coverage at 1-2% of covered equipment value per year, and a 50 MW hall carries roughly $50-80M of gensets, UPS, chillers and switchgear, so about $0.5-1.6M of annual premium per hall and roughly $100-300K of commission to the MGA. That is on the order of 5-10x the parent's audit fee per hall.
non_obvious_insight: The inspection is both the revenue product and the underwriting filter, and the two feed each other. Defects found pre-expiry are paid by the OEM, which reduces adverse selection, and the resulting data is a cornered resource: independent, fleet-level, load-based, across OEMs. The parent treated the warranty as an asset to recover. The bigger business treats post-warranty risk as an asset class to price, using the only thing OEMs cannot easily replicate, which is neutral cross-vendor test data.
first_30_days: Draft a two-page Load-Proven protocol with a load-bank rental partner and a NETA-type test firm. Get one data-center-finance law firm or lender's technical advisor to review a one-page covenant template. Pitch three owners with halls approaching OEM expiry and one lender with a delayed-lease loan. Meet two equipment-breakdown or specialty warranty MGAs and ask what data they would need to quote a quota-share on tested MEP gear. Goal: one paid pilot test signed and one written indication of appetite from a capacity provider.

title: Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings
one_liner: Remove the half-day minimum by dispatching remote stenographers into many short hearings per day, so a family-law litigant gets a certified record of a 15-minute hearing for about $100.
customer: California family law and probate attorneys and solo practitioners. Self-represented litigants reached through DV legal aid organizations and family law facilitators. Legal aid groups buying bulk credits. Later, county courts contracting to meet the new duty to provide records to indigent litigants.
problem: California logged roughly 3 million civil, family and probate hearings without a verbatim record between April 2023 and March 2026, about 7 in 10. Without a record, appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail, because the appellant cannot show error. Private reporters charge $250-$500+ appearance minimums, since a reporter can wait 2-3 hours for a 12-minute calendar item. Nobody pays that for a routine hearing. In 2026 the California Supreme Court (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) held that courts must give indigent litigants an official verbatim record on request, and courts do not have the reporters to comply.
solution: A dispatch platform that reads court calendars, predicts when each matter will be called from historical hearing-type durations per department, and pages a remote reporter into the court's Zoom or Teams feed only for the minutes needed. One reporter covers 8-12 short hearings a day across departments. Deliver a certified transcript in 24-72 hours, with an AI first draft for the reporter to scope. Price is a flat $95 for hearings up to 15 minutes and about $8 per page beyond that. Start where remote appearance and remote reporting are allowed (California's AB 3013 authorizes remote reporting, and each court's procedures need checking). Pitch courts on per-department-day capacity at a discount to staffing a full-time reporter.
why_now: The 2026 California Supreme Court ruling creates a legal duty courts cannot currently meet. AB 3013 (2024) opened remote reporting. The workforce is projected to be about 5,500 reporters short by 2030. Family courts are widely on video. Reporter dead time is a scheduling problem that software can solve.
revenue_model: Per-hearing fees paid by attorneys and litigants. Bulk credits funded by legal aid and foundation grants. Later B2G contracts priced per courtroom-day. The reporter keeps about 55-60% of each hearing fee, which beats their typical hourly yield because dead time is eliminated.
non_obvious_insight: The reporter shortage is partly a utilization problem. In a busy family calendar department, a reporter may write 2-3 hours of a 7-hour day and wait the rest. Remote hopping sells that dead time to several litigants at once, so the price can fall 70% while the reporter earns more.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 remote-capable freelance or semi-retired reporters. Pick one county whose family departments run on Zoom and cover it manually with a shared spreadsheet and a text pager. Offer 10 solo family law attorneys and two DV appellate nonprofits (start with the Family Violence Appellate Project) at-cost coverage of their next 5 hearings. Track wait time per hearing so the prediction model has real data.

Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind.

title: Grid-Readiness Model Audit for Data Center Lenders
one_liner: An independent checker for private-credit funds, banks and delay-in-start-up insurers that audits a borrower's large-load models and ride-through evidence and gives an energization-risk opinion, the same way financial-model auditors already serve project-finance lenders.
customer: Data center and GPU-cloud finance teams at credit funds, banks and ABS arrangers, plus the lender's independent engineers, technical advisors and project-finance law firms that act as the channel. Delay-in-start-up (DSU) insurers and MGAs are the second payer. The borrower's fee is paid at lender direction, which is the market norm for lender advisors.
problem: Lenders finance billions of dollars of campuses and GPU fleets. Interest accrues and hardware depreciates while the site waits for energization. Their diligence covers construction cost, schedule, MEP and offtake, but grid dynamic behavior is a black box authored by an interested party: the borrower's own consultant says interconnection is on track. After the 2024 Northern Virginia load-loss event and ERCOT's new rules, lenders have no independent way to judge whether the load model will pass, whether ride-through settings will trip the site, or how far energization could slip. Developer-side consultants such as Electranix and Danovo are conflicted, and the lender's independent engineer typically lacks EMT skills.
solution:
Sell a check, not a build.
1) A pre-close Grid-Readiness Opinion of $30-75k per site. It is an independent review of the borrower's PSS/E and EMT models, study reports, interconnection-agreement conditions and UPS, PSU and firmware settings against the ISO's rules and generic reference models. It ends with a red/amber/green rating and a P50/P90 energization-slip range.
2) A conditions-precedent and covenant kit for law firms: draw conditions such as ISO-accepted model, passed ride-through test and firmware freeze.
3) Re-attestation of $10-20k whenever GPU generation or UPS firmware changes, triggered by covenant.
4) A portfolio dashboard for lenders by ISO and site, and an anonymized risk dataset for DSU underwriters.
Analysts run rule-based checklists and scripted checks through the PSS/E Python API, so each review takes about 40-80 hours. Our own modeling is never required.
why_now: Neocloud and data center debt (delayed-draw term loans, GPU-backed facilities, ABS) grew explosively in 2025-26, and energization delay has become a visible schedule risk in publicly reported neocloud results. Regulatory rules that make models and ride-through a gating item are now in force in Texas, with PJM and NERC large-load work following. Lenders and insurers are looking for a diligence item to price, and nobody offers it yet.
revenue_model: Borrower-paid, lender-directed fees of $30-75k per site per financing and $10-20k per refresh re-attestation. DSU insurers pay $10-25k per underwriting review, or a data license, and later take a share of premium through an MGA program. Rough bottom-up: 200 qualifying US financings a year (assumption to verify) at $50k is about $10M, and 400 sites refreshed at $15k is about $6M, so this is a $15-25M niche. It is a thin, high-margin analyst business that later becomes a rating or registry.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer of a grid model is whoever bears the cost of delay, not the grid. Project finance already has an independent-checker culture, with financial-model audits and independent engineers, because lenders will not trust numbers authored by the borrower. A dynamic load model is the same kind of black-box spreadsheet driving a billion-dollar decision. The parent's three structural threats become tailwinds here. Free EPRI or NERC generic models become the benchmark we audit against. OEM secrecy is irrelevant because we test the borrower's model against acceptance criteria and measured behavior and need no OEM IP. In-house hyperscaler tools do not matter because hyperscalers are not project-financed on this basis. Independence is the moat, which the developer-side consultants cannot claim.
first_30_days: Run 15 interviews: 5 data center finance leads at credit funds and banks, 5 lender independent engineers or technical advisors, 3 DSU underwriters or brokers, and 2 project-finance law firms. Offer a $25k pilot Grid-Readiness Opinion on one live financing. Sign one independent-engineer firm as a white-label channel, since it can bill our add-on and lacks EMT capability. Recruit one ex-ISO planner and one project-finance analyst. Publish a 20-question Grid-Readiness Diligence Checklist for lenders and a redacted sample opinion built from public queue and rule data, and pass it through law firms as collateral.

title: Section-Level Hydrogen and Helium Leads for Landmen
one_liner: Sell 90-day exclusive, page-linked lists of Nemaha-corridor sections with hydrogen or helium evidence buried in old mud logs, DST reports and driller notes, to the landmen and lease shops who spend the first dollars of every junior's program.
customer: Independent landmen and lease-brokerage shops (2-50 people) in Kansas, Nebraska and Oklahoma who assemble acreage for natural hydrogen and helium juniors, plus the roughly 40-120 junior explorers themselves (Rystad counts 40, AKAP counts 123 companies). Wedge buyer: the lease shop, because it is paid per acre leased, has a hard deadline (leases are taken in a rush after each well announcement), and has no geoscientist on staff.
problem: The free datasets (USGS/BLM 16,000 gas analyses, KGS OFR 2025-59, SMU/GDR temperatures) already give away the structured layers, so an atlas built on them is worthless. What they omit is the unstructured evidence in page images at KCC/KGS-type archives: mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test gas notes, driller remarks such as 'gas would not burn', 'non-flammable' or 'heavy N2 odor', and water-well gas notes. Landmen today pick where to lease by copying the footprint of the last press release, which means they arrive after the price of a lease has already moved. Juniors that do this in-house (HyTerra, MAX Power, Koloma) are not customers, so the sellable market is the long tail and the lease shops serving it.
solution: A curated evidence-card product for one live fairway (Nemaha Uplift and Midcontinent Rift, KS/NE/OK). A VLM pipeline reads page images for a defined set of document types, a geologist verifies every card that reaches a customer, and each card carries the page image, the quoted text, and a confidence grade for sampling method, air-contamination signs (N2/O2 ratio) and analytical era. Cards roll up to a ranked list of 30-60 sections per block, plus a short 'do not lease' list of sections with clean hydrocarbon gas and no signal, which saves buyers money. Free layers (USGS, KGS, BLM/state mineral ownership) are ingested as baseline and shown for context but never sold. Delivered as a GeoPackage/KMZ and a PDF, with a courtroom-simple audit trail so a landman can defend the pick to a junior's board. Geothermal is dropped from v1 because SMU/GDR and GeoMap give it away.
why_now: Natural hydrogen went from about 10 to 40+ searching companies since 2020 (Rystad) and 123 by AKAP's count; HyTerra's Kansas McCoy 1 result (up to 83-96% H2) turned the Nemaha corridor into an active lease play in 2025-26, so lease shops need defensible picks right now. VLMs now read typed and handwritten well forms at cents per page, which broke the cost barrier that made a section-level re-read uneconomic before 2024. State surveys (KGS/KCC) are releasing more scans, and the academic OCR/LLM methods are public, which lowers the technical risk for a two-person team while making curation and speed the real product.
revenue_model: Entry pack: $5k non-exclusive, 3-township block. Exclusive block: $12-20k for a 90-day first-look on a 6-10 township block, renewable. Success fee: a capped per-net-acre finder fee (for example $2-5) or 0.5% ORRI on leases taken from exclusive-block sections. Year-1 bottom-up: 25 entry packs ($125k) + 6 exclusive blocks ($90k) + fees (~$50k) is about $265k with a two-person team; the business scales by adding fairways (Michigan/Ohio Rift extension, Colorado, Texas Panhandle helium) rather than by raising price per corridor. The buyer's ROI check: a 20,000-acre lease program at even $20-50/acre bonus is $0.4-1M, so a $5-15k pack is single-digit percent of spend.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not data, it is time-boxed scarcity. Lease information is perishable: once one buyer signs, the price of that section moves, so the value of a lead decays over weeks, and the right pricing unit is a 90-day exclusive option on a block, exactly how prospect generators sell in oil and gas. Second, the 0.5% hit rate seen in the Paris Basin OCR study (26 wells of about 5,000) is a weakness for a broad atlas but a strength for a precision shortlist: sell 40 sections, not 40,000, and let the 'do not lease' list carry the rest of the value. Third, buyers who drill a lead and share the result get a discount, and those results become a private ground-truth set that calibrates the confidence score, which no free dataset can copy.

Week 2: have a geologist verify the top 150 candidate cards and produce a 60-section block map with page-image links. Week 3: contact 10 lease shops and 10 juniors (LinkedIn plus the AAPL and Kansas Independent Oil and Gas Association member lists) with one free sample card and a demo map. Week 4: ask for a $5k prepay for the block pack. Kill test from the parent: if fewer than 3 of 10 prepay, stop and go to the state-survey channel instead. Also offer an exclusive 90-day option on the sections buyers like best.
