title: A Price Reporting Agency for Trade Materials
one_liner: Turn pooled supply-house invoices into contract-grade, SKU-level price evidence for the trades, starting with cost-change certificates that win price-adjustment change orders and ending as the index that escalation clauses and price-lock guarantees reference.
customer: First: plumbing, HVAC and electrical subcontractors with $3-30M revenue that carry fixed-price bids, multi-month jobs and maintenance agreements and eat cost changes between bid and buy. End state: the counterparties who write and argue escalation clauses, meaning general contractors, property owners and managers, municipal procurement, insurers, home-warranty programs, lenders, and the manufacturers and distributors who want realized-price data.
problem: Price adjustment requests are argued with anecdotes. A sub says copper fittings and water heaters are up 15-20% since the bid, and the GC or owner asks for proof. Broad public benchmarks (producer price indices and estimating books) are category-level and lag what contractors actually pay by SKU at their contractor multiplier in their region, and supplier price letters flow to contractors with a long lag, as the parent's tariff research noted (50% Section 232 copper duty from August 1, 2025). Subs either absorb the difference on fixed-price work or lose weeks assembling invoices by hand. There is no independent, contract-grade reference that both sides of a contract accept, as far as the parent's research and I could find. Parent idea limit: a per-shop audit keeps price data private and never becomes anything a counterparty trusts.
solution: Step 1 (months 0-6) sells a Cost-Change Certificate. For a sub with a fixed-price contract or bid, we parse its own supplier invoices and quotes into a SKU-normalized evidence pack: cost at the bid date versus cost at purchase, supplier price-letter references, invoice copies, and the escalation amount calculated by the contract's own formula, reviewed by the shop's accountant. It needs no network on day one, only one shop's invoices. Step 2: every certificate is paid partly in data, since the shop opts in to contribute its anonymized line items to the pool and in exchange gets a free alert feed ('your PEX-A fitting cost is 9% above the regional median'). Step 3 (months 6-18): publish weekly transaction-based indices by category and region, with a 30-day lag, minimum-contributor thresholds, no supplier or shop names, to stay clear of price-signaling and confidentiality problems. Owners, GCs and municipalities start writing 'adjusted per [Index] Copper Fittings, Region' into contracts and pay for verified access. Step 4 (months 18-36): price-lock guarantees for quoted jobs, underwritten off the index through an MGA or reinsurer partner, where shops pay a small premium on covered materials and we carry the basis risk we understand better than anyone.
why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings made price adjustment a routine dispute in 2025-26, and owners and GCs are rewriting price-adjustment language. The barrier to a transaction index was always normalizing hundreds of supplier catalog and invoice formats into comparable SKUs, and LLMs just made that cheap. Field-service and accounting systems make invoice ingestion easy. The volatility also means the certificate solves a painful, dated, dollar-denominated problem today, not a theoretical data project.
revenue_model: Certificates at $250-400 each, or 15-20% of the escalation actually approved (better alignment on big claims). Then index subscriptions of $500-2,000 per month for GCs, owners, insurers and municipal buyers who want verified reference access, with data licensing to manufacturers and distributors for realized-price and sell-through data. Later underwriting margin on price-lock guarantees, priced at roughly 1.5-3% of covered materials. Example: a sub with a $400K contract that is 30% materials and 8% higher-cost has a $9,600 claim, and a 20% success fee on half of that approved is about $1,000 per contract.
non_obvious_insight: In commodity markets the durable business is not the data feed but being the named reference in contracts, which is why price reporting agencies for metals and lumber have switching costs no feed provider has. The way in is not a dashboard. It is a document that ends an argument, sold to the party who is losing money now. The certificate requires no network on day one, and the network appears as a byproduct because every certificate adds contributed data. It is also a position platform vendors and supply houses structurally cannot take. ServiceTitan and Kojo depend on supplier integrations such as Ferguson and Hajoca, and publishing cross-customer price data pits those partners against their users, while a supply house cannot publish its own multipliers.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 light-commercial mechanical and plumbing subs with open fixed-price contracts where costs have risen since bid (owner peer groups, PHCC and ACCA chapters). Build the SKU normalizer for the top 200 SKUs (copper tube and fittings, PEX, PVC, water heaters, gas flex) across Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply, Home Depot Pro and local-house formats. Produce 5 certificates within 2 weeks and record how each GC or owner responds, since approval rate and dollars approved are the key learning. Sign 3 shops to the contingency version. Publish a free monthly 'copper fittings' note from the first shops' data (with disclosure) to seed the brand. Have an attorney review the contribution agreement and the aggregation and lag rules before publishing anything pooled. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so verify that no existing indices or claim-documentation vendors serve this niche.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. It also moves the monetization away from the crowded supplier-invoice audit toward evidence and a standard, where the incumbents have no product.

title: Dual-Mode Genset Permits for Queued Campuses
one_liner: Design the air permit for new data center campuses before the generators are bought, so the backup fleet is legally curtailment-ready from day one and the fee is tied to energization date.
customer: Energy and development leads at spec developers, powered-shell builders and neocloud/colo operators with 50-400 MW campuses in PJM (AEP Ohio, Dominion, ComEd, PPL). The wedge is campuses that have filed, or are about to file, their air-permit application and have not yet placed genset purchase orders. Hyperscalers with in-house permitting teams are excluded at first. Air consultants are a secondary channel.
problem: The parent's real cost is retrofitting existing Tier 2 emergency fleets. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), emergency engines are capped at 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of that can earn income or serve a financial arrangement. Reclassifying an installed fleet means stricter engine standards, re-permitting and public comment. Yet the largest cohort of new engines is being permitted right now as emergency-only, because that is the cheapest and fastest path. That choice locks out capacity and curtailment use for 15 or more years. PJM's curtail-or-bring-capacity direction means those same campuses will need on-site backup to energize earlier. Nobody is designing the permit for that second use at the moment the choice is cheap.
solution: A fixed-price 'Dual-Mode Permit Package' sold before genset purchase orders and inside the air-permit comment window. (1) A one-time state legal feasibility memo from a retained air attorney (VA, OH, IL, PA), which gates every engagement. (2) An engine spec that is Tier 4 Final or SCR-ready, with catalyst and urea footprint reserved, ECM hour-metering and paralleling ready. This turns retrofit financing into a spec change costing a fraction of a retrofit. (3) Permit application language and modeling: an emergency mode plus a capped grid-emergency/curtailment mode of roughly 100-200 hours, synthetic-minor NOx limits, 1-hour NO2 dispersion modeling, and a community disclosure plan. (4) A curtailment-readiness dossier the utility and PJM can cite when offering earlier or flexible energization. Engines are certified as non-emergency-capable from the start, so the campus never has to fight the emergency-to-non-emergency reclassification.
why_now: Turbines are sold out until roughly 2029-30, so the practical path to earlier energization is on-site capacity that can be built now. PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short, and the connect-and-manage and bring-your-own-capacity framework is being filed at FERC. Large OEM gensets with SCR options are catalog items, and campuses energizing in 2028-30 must order engines and file permits in the next 6-12 months. This would not have worked in 2019, when there was no curtailment penalty for missing on-site capacity.
revenue_model: $60-150k fixed fee per campus (feasibility memo, spec, permit drafting, modeling). A success fee applies when the permit issues with the dual-mode condition (about $50k), and a further one applies only when the utility or PJM offers earlier or flexible energization that cites the dossier, at roughly $1-2k per MW per month of acceleration. A 200 MW campus energized six months early is worth about $1-2M to us. A colo campus that size earns on the order of $30M a month at full lease-up, so the buyer's return is 50x or more. An optional 10% share of capacity revenue for five years is secondary. Illustrative unit economics: 10 campuses in year one is roughly $1.5-3M, with two lawyers, two engineers and one permit modeler.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest time to unlock diesel is before it exists. The permit design is a one-time, 15-year decision, and taking it at application costs a fraction of a retrofit. It turns the parent's hardest problem (retrofit financing plus reclassification risk) into a purchase-spec problem that the buyer is already paying for. It also changes what is being sold, from capacity revenue that the buyer discounts to time. Energization date is the metric a developer's CFO already tracks, and every month of delay costs more than any capacity payment. Public permit dockets show exactly which campuses are in the window, so lead generation is a scrape rather than cold outreach.
first_30_days: Week 1: commission the air-attorney feasibility memo ($8-10k), covering which engine and classification path works in VA, OH, IL and PA. If no path closes at Tier 4 or SCR cost, stop. Weeks 1-2: scrape VA DEQ, Ohio EPA, IEPA and PA DEP public notices for data center genset permit applications filed in the last 12 months (target 40) and identify the developer and the consultant of record for each. Weeks 2-4: cold-contact the development leads and offer a $12k 'dual-mode gap review' of the pending application inside the public comment window. In parallel, offer the applicants' air consultants a white-label subcontract for the dual-mode module. Aim for two paid gap reviews and one campus package LOI. The demand test is whether a developer will pay before PO to keep the option open.
lineage: mutation of I0836 ('Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead. | How this version avoids them: Trinity-type consultancies sell reactive, hourly permit work, are not tied to capacity or energization outcomes, and do not spec engines. We offer them the dual-mode module as a white-label add-on rather than compete. Voltus and CPower can only enroll resources that are already dual-mode, so we are their upstream and never touch enrollment or the DR revenue relationship. ERock sells gas hardware and a bridge-to-grid story. We are engine-agnostic and ride on gensets the campus must buy anyway, so there is no incremental hardware capex to finance. We also avoid the parent's unproven retrofit-of-Tier-2 step and its legal trap by working only on greenfield permits, and we gate on the attorney memo.

title: Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data
one_liner: An audit that tells research buyers what share of their online-panel responses came from bots, agents or fraud farms, and recalibrates the study against a verified-human control sample.
customer: Insights heads at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms, UX-research teams, academic labs and pollsters who buy panel sample from third-party vendors at $5-500 per complete.
problem: One prompt to a commercial AI agent now passes screeners and attention checks. A controlled evaluation found synthetic respondents passing 99.8% of 6,000 attention-check trials. As little as 3-7% contaminated responses can invalidate conclusions. Panel vendors both sell the sample and score its quality, so buyers cannot trust the referee.
solution: A per-study data-quality audit. Response files (timings, paradata, device data, open-ends) go through a detection ensemble plus honeypot items. A subset of the same questionnaire goes to a small address-recruited, device-attested human panel as a ground-truth control. Deliver an audit stamp, contamination-adjusted estimates, and a vendor scorecard across suppliers.
why_now: Survey-fraud research in 2025-26 shows agents beating attention checks. An MIT-run $50K challenge is testing detection, and NORC published a fraud literature review. Election-season polling and pharma sample budgets raise the stakes, and buyers are asking who audits the panels.
revenue_model: $3-15k per study audit, $50-150k per year programmes for insights teams that spend $2-10M on sample, and vendor-scorecard subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Most anti-fraud tooling is sold by panel sellers, whose incentive is to under-report fraud. The scarce asset is not detection code but an independent, verified-human comparison group, because you cannot prove what is fake without a known-real reference.
first_30_days: Recruit about 2,000 verified humans by address-based mail or a university survey-centre partnership. Buy sample from six panel vendors yourself and publish a 'state of sample quality' benchmark. Offer free audits to five insights leaders who have posted about bad data.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight.

title: Insurer-Paid Total-Loss Add-On Refund Concierge
one_liner: When a financed car is totaled, the auto insurer's settlement packet is exactly what GAP and service-contract administrators demand, so the insurer pays a flat fee to have every unearned add-on refund and GAP claim filed and tracked for the claimant, who keeps 100 percent of the money.
customer: Personal-auto insurers' total-loss claims and claims-experience leaders, starting with regional and mutual carriers (roughly 50K to 1M policies; dozens to low hundreds of them, estimate) and independent-agency channels, reached through total-loss valuation and claims-platform vendors and claims TPAs as channel partners. The claimant is the beneficiary; the insurer is the payer.
problem: About one in five collision claims ends in a total loss (2M+ vehicles a year, estimate; verify with CCC-type data). Many of those cars are financed and carry rolled-in GAP, service contracts, tire-and-wheel, paint and key products that are worthless the day the car is totaled. Unearned pro-rata refunds are owed and GAP may pay a deficiency, but each has deadlines and document demands (valuation report, settlement letter, proof of loss date, payoff letter). The dealer that sold the products is long gone, the lender only sees a payoff, and the insurer never touches the retail installment contract. The claimant, already at peak frustration with the insurer, leaves money on the table, then shops for the next car and the next policy.
solution: A link in the total-loss settlement email or adjuster portal. The claimant photographs the retail installment contract (or uploads the payoff letter and dealer bill of sale). LLM extraction lists the financed add-ons and administrators; the engine computes refunds owed as of the date of loss under the contract and state rules and flags any possible GAP claim; it then auto-assembles the packet using the insurer's own valuation report, settlement letter and loss date, submits to each administrator, chases to payment, and escalates stalled cases to the state insurance department. The claimant sees a live tracker and receives 100% of recovered money (or it reduces the payoff if the loan is open, per contract). The insurer gets a dashboard of dollars recovered, days to pay and complaints avoided.
why_now: Total-loss frequency is at record levels as repair costs outpace vehicle values. Insurers just lived through 2023 to 2025 record rate increases and policyholder shopping, so retention after a claim is now a board-level metric. Claims workflows are digital end to end (e-settlement letters, text-based claims), so a link fits where a call center never did. LLMs read contract scans and administrator forms for cents, and 84-month loans with stacked add-ons mean more claimants carry unearned products than in 2019.
revenue_model: Insurer pays only for completed value: about $45 per claim where a refund or GAP payment is recovered, plus a $60K to $150K annual platform fee for integration and dashboards at a mid-size carrier (estimates to test). Channel partners take 20 to 30 percent of revenue. Illustration: a regional insurer with 8,000 total losses a year, 20% eligible with financed add-ons, is 1,600 cases at $45, about $72K a year plus platform fee. The claimant is never charged. Later modules: replacement-vehicle loan referral and title chase, and sold benchmarks of administrator refund and GAP payment speed to insurer vendor-management teams and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The parent assumed the lender's payoff desk is the one place that sees the loan end. Total loss is a second such moment, and there the insurer, not the lender, holds the documents administrators need and has the motive to make the claimant whole. Because the insurer's paper carries a valuation report and loss date, administrators cannot stall on it the way they stall on a consumer's cancellation request. The insurer's motive is retention and complaint ratio, not the refund itself, so the fee-optics problem disappears (nobody skims the claimant's money), and the purchase comes from a claims-experience budget that already exists rather than a compliance budget that must be fought for.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2: build the refund and GAP-claim rules engine for the 15 largest administrators, the claimant flow and the insurer letter template. Weeks 1 to 4: pitch 10 independent insurance agencies (who feel post-loss churn directly), 3 regional or mutual insurer claims VPs and 2 claims-technology partners. Offer a free 60-day pilot on 100 total-loss claimants with a signed LOI at $45 per recovered case if average recovery exceeds $500. Run the first 30 to 50 claimants as a concierge (analyst plus LLM), tracking opt-in rate, share with financed add-ons, average dollars and days to pay. Publish a one-page 'what a total loss leaves on the table' note from those numbers to open insurer doors.

Competitor check: GAP.    - A per-payoff, lender-integrated refund workflow for dealer-sold, financed add-ons at credit unions.

   - CU vendor due diligence and core/LOS integration will make the sales cycle slow.
   - The California SB 766 citation in the idea did not check out. The leginfo summary I fetched for the 2023-24 bill described an unrelated social-worker licensing bill. Do not rely on that cite until it is confirmed. | How this version avoids them: There is no lender integration, so Origence-style LOS vendors and credit-union procurement do not matter. Consumer refund sites depend on the borrower finding them after the fact and lack the insurer's valuation letter; here outreach lands in the settlement packet on day zero. Administrators such as Assurant are the party asked to pay, not a buyer, and the insurer's paper and regulator relationships make stalling costly. Lenders' in-house recovery teams work repossessions and charge-offs, not current-pay total losses, so there is no overlap. Claims-tech valuation and settlement vendors are channel partners because they neither read contracts nor know administrator rules; the risk is one of them building it, so lock a distribution partnership early. title: Scribe-Adjusted EBITDA: Privileged Diligence for Physician Deals
one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-business-day, counsel-engaged report that tells private equity buyers how much of a scribe-enabled physician group's revenue is real, and what the rest could cost them.
customer: Deal partners and VPs at lower-middle-market PE funds and MSOs buying 20-150 provider specialty groups (dermatology, orthopedics, ophthalmology, GI, urology, behavioral health, primary care) that adopted an ambient scribe in the last 18 months. The engaging party is the buyer's healthcare transactions counsel, so the work is privileged. Quality-of-earnings accounting firms are channel partners, not rivals.
problem: Buyers pay a multiple of EBITDA that now includes scribe-era E/M uplift, and drift dollars fall through at near-100% margin. Illustration (assumptions to validate): $30M revenue, 40% E/M, 6% scribe uplift gives $0.72M, about 14% of a $5M EBITDA, or roughly $8M of enterprise value at 11x. A stock deal also inherits overpayment liability, and the 60-day return rule starts once a problem is identified. Nobody in the deal team can answer the question. QoE accountants have no coder bench. Regulatory counsel runs generic billing samples. Seller materials and scribe vendor 'AAPC-verified' claims are self-serving. The parent's own research flags that the drift may be legitimate documentation catch-up, so buyers cannot tell whether to discount it or trust it.
solution: Deliverable is a 'Scribe-Adjusted Run-Rate Report', engaged through deal counsel under a privilege-preserving engagement letter. (1) Causal drift estimate: 24-36 months of claims from the data room plus each provider's scribe go-live date from the seller's admin console. Because rollouts are staggered, non-adopters and late adopters in the same group form a built-in control group, so a staggered difference-in-differences replaces a naive before/after. (2) Coder-signed sample: 150-300 stratified encounters from the highest-drift providers, reviewed by certified coders on MDM and time statements. This splits drift into 'supported catch-up' and 'at-risk narration'. (3) Outputs: a scribe-adjusted EBITDA range, an extrapolated overpayment exposure with a confidence interval, and recommended escrow, specific indemnity or price adjustment language. It also includes a 100-day post-close remediation and refund plan. (4) Later: the same report sold sell-side ('prove your uplift is clean before you go to market') to cut re-trades.
why_now: Scribes went mainstream across groups in 2025-26, so the first wave of PE deals with 12-24 months of scribe-era claims is closing now. Payers have begun automated E/M downcoding (Cigna's nationwide policy from October 2025 is reported), so uplift in the trailing run-rate may not persist. The FCA enforcement climate makes successor liability a live diligence topic. There is no historical playbook, because this diligence item did not exist in 2023.
revenue_model: $20-45k per buy-side report, priced by provider count and data volume. $8-15k for a sell-side readiness version. Optional 100-day post-close monitor at $4-8k per month. Direct cost is roughly $3-5k per report (30-45 coder hours plus senior review), so gross margin is about 80%. Two people can deliver one to two reports a week. A benchmark subscription for funds is a later add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Two things. First, the buyer does not need the scribe to be wrong. They need a number, and the staggered rollout gives each target its own control group, which the drift studies with pre/post design and the free-diagnostic framing in the parent both miss. Second, EBITDA leverage makes a $30k report protect about $8M of price, so it is priced against the deal, not against a compliance budget. The same report is also valuable to a seller with clean documentation, which makes it a two-sided product that gets better as deals accumulate.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build a public-data pre-screen from the CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service file (updated May 2026). It shows each NPI's E/M level mix by year for any target roster. Public data means no client claims and no privilege problem, but the year lag means it only catches early adopters, so the full report needs data-room claims. Retain a healthcare regulatory attorney to draft the privileged engagement template, and contract 2 CPC/CPMA coders. Days 8-30: contact 25 healthcare-transactions lawyers at mid-market firms and 20 lower-middle-market PE healthcare associates, offering a free public-data pre-screen on any target they are bidding on under NDA. Aim for one paid confirmatory-diligence pilot at $12-15k, in exchange for the right to keep de-identified aggregate statistics and a reference.
lineage: mutation of I0389 ('Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface. | How this version avoids them: VMG Health is the incumbent most able to copy this, because it does transaction-side valuation and compliance work. The defense is packaging, not technology: a narrow fixed-price 10-day product built around a causal design, delivered through deal counsel, plus a deal-by-deal benchmark of typical uplift by scribe vendor and specialty that grows with each engagement. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer, MDaudit and Healthicity are software sold to a practice's in-house compliance team on an annual cycle. In diligence the practice is the seller, so the buyer is different and the clock is different. Scribe vendors (Ambience, Abridge, DeepScribe) and autonomous coders (Fathom, Arintra, CodaMetrix) self-attest, so a buyer cannot rely on them. Trilliant and BCBSA publish the drift and define what a payer will challenge, but neither sells a per-target answer. Our report resolves the 'may be legitimate documentation catch-up' caveat that Trilliant itself raises.

title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors.

title: Widow-First Retention Drills for Wealth Advisors
one_liner: Sell independent advisors an annual 'if one of us dies' rehearsal for couples, because the defection risk sits at the first spouse's death, not with the kids.
customer: Independent RIAs and small wealth teams ($150M-$2B AUM) whose median client is 65+. The buyer is the firm principal or COO.
problem: The industry spends on next-gen events with heirs. Cerulli says about $54T of the transfer is spousal and about $40T of that goes to widowed women. The survivor is grieving, holds a house full of logins and unknown accounts, and has to decide whether to keep the advisor. Advisors are commonly said to lose most widows within a year (widely cited, verify). The cause is usually friction, not performance.
solution: A 90-minute 'Survivor Fire Drill' run by the advisor's team with a software kit. Each spouse's death is simulated in turn. The tool builds a First-90-Days playbook: who to call, which accounts exist, which autopays must keep running, and where the documents are. It audits titling and beneficiaries from the survivor's point of view and flags single points of failure, such as only one spouse knowing the passwords. It then schedules pre-agreed advisor check-ins at day 3, 14, 45 and 90. The advisor gets a dashboard of which couples have done the drill and where their exposure is.
why_now: Cerulli's Sept 2026 work frames retention of the transfer as the priority, and 89% of surveyed firms call family meetings essential. Wealth managers are buying heir-engagement tools, yet the first wave of money is spousal and the widow is under-served. Cheap document ingestion and secure vaults make the kit affordable for small firms.
revenue_model: $300-$700 per household per year billed to the firm, or a $25-40K/yr platform fee for a 100-household book. The ROI pitch: keeping one $1.5M widow at a 1% fee is worth $15K a year.
non_obvious_insight: The heir-retention narrative aims at the wrong person on the wrong day. Widows rarely leave over portfolio returns. They leave because nobody made the first 90 days easy. A rehearsal also works where estate planning fails, because people avoid 'planning' but will attend a scheduled drill.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 RIAs through advisor communities and podcasts. Run drills by hand with a spreadsheet and printed binder for each firm's 10 oldest couples. Record time-to-locate-accounts and the number of single-point-of-failure findings. Charge a $2.5K pilot fee and turn the findings into a retention case study the advisor can show prospects.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Empathy (LifeVault + Loss Support), Everplans (Enterprise / advisor channel), Trustworthy (Family Operating System), Wealth.com. White space: Nobody found sells the specific wedge: a facilitated, scheduled couples rehearsal of the first spouse's death, run by the advisor's team. That means simulating each spouse's death in turn with the surviving spouse actually doing the tasks; a survivor-point-of-view audit of titling, beneficiaries, autopays and password single points of failure; pre-agreed day 3/14/45/90 advisor check-ins; and a firm dashboard of drill completion and exposure. Vaults (Empathy, Everplans, Trustworthy) and estate-document platforms (Wealth.com, Vanilla) store information and generate documents, but their pages describe no behavioral ritual, no survivor-POV stress test and no post-death outreach cadence. Independent RIAs at $150M-$2B AUM are also not Empathy's core buyer (insurers, banks and big wealth firms). Caveats: I did not confirm that Empathy lacks scheduled outreach (its Connect page 404'd), and I could not check consultant-led widow-retention programs (see the note under evidence_of_demand). The software layer is commoditized (Trustworthy at $10 per client per year), so the defensible white space is the ritual, the audit method and the outreach cadence, not the vault.

title: Rotor Rescue: Scrapyard Magnet Pick-and-Pay
one_liner: A price-sheet-plus-gauss-meter program that pays scrapyards for magnet-dense motors and rotors they currently sell as steel and copper.
customer: Rare-earth magnet recyclers and magnet makers needing domestic recycled feed (they pay per kg with assay). Scrapyards, motor rebuilders and appliance/HVAC recyclers are the sellers.
problem: The rare-earth bottleneck is 'collection and disassembly rather than recovery chemistry.' Hard-drive magnet removal often costs more than the material is worth. Yards sell EV drive units, servo and elevator motors, and e-bike hub motors by copper and steel weight, and the NdFeB rotors go into the steel shred.
solution: Skip HDDs and target a short list of heavy, magnet-dense items. Yards get a phone app plus a $150 gauss meter that identifies magnet-bearing units and shows a payout per unit or per rotor. A mobile pull cell or the yard's own labor removes rotors. We aggregate and assay them, then sell a certified, traceable magnet-feed stream to recyclers.
why_now: The IEA puts China at about 90% of material recovery capacity. The DoD-MP deal and the Texas magnet campus create domestic pull, and DOE announced $134M for critical-mineral demonstrations in June 2026. Recyclers such as Cyclic Materials and IonicRE are funded and need feed.
revenue_model: Spread between the recycler's price per kg of assayed magnet feed and the yard payout plus pull cost. Optional premium for defense-traceable lots. Small SaaS fee for the identification and price app.
non_obvious_insight: Rare-earth economics fail on tiny magnets (HDDs) but work on a few heavy items. No one publishes a price by motor model, so yards do not know a rotor holds hundreds of grams to kilograms of NdFeB. Price discovery is the missing product, not a new chemistry.
first_30_days: Buy 5 gauss meters. Visit 10 auto shredders and motor shops and measure and photograph 200 units. Build a price sheet by model. Get an offtake LOI from one magnet recycler that needs feed. Pay 3 yards on the first 50 units and publish the results to recruit more.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Cyclic Materials, HyProMag USA (CoTec / Mkango JV), ERI (Electronics Recyclers International), Noveon Magnetics. White space: Evidence caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran zero successful web searches and relied on direct page fetches of about 20 company and source URLs. Several were 404, 503 or blocked. Coverage of forums, RFPs, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and open-source tools is therefore missing. Treat this as a partial check, not a clean bill of health.

What remains unserved, judged from the company pages I could read:
(1) A yard-facing price and identification product. No fetched page (Cyclic, HyProMag, ReElement, Ionic, Noveon) publishes a payout by motor make and model, a magnet-mass lookup, or a handheld gauss-meter workflow for yard staff. Cyclic's supplier page explicitly gives no pricing, logistics or ID tools ('contact us to get started').
(2) The long tail of small and mid-size auto shredders, motor rebuilders, elevator and industrial motor shops, and e-bike hub-motor scrap. ERI is anchored on e-waste and the OEM/ITAD channel, and Cyclic's named categories are drive motors, HDDs, robotics, defense and wind. Elevator, servo and e-bike hub motors are not named.
(3) Chain-of-custody and assay data for defense-traceable lots.

Where the idea is weak: the buyers are building their own procurement. Cyclic takes whole units without dismantling, so the 'mobile pull cell' adds little. Cyclic and HyProMag have stated supply pipelines and can capture the aggregator margin by paying yards directly once yards know what they hold. The spread-based aggregator model is exposed to that squeeze. The durable wedge is the data and identification layer.
